summary.text: Factorial splitting expresses the successive binomial coefficients through reduced-residue products \(G_c(m)=\prod_{p\nmid t,\,t<p^m}(t+c p^m)\); pairing \(t\) with \(p^m-t\), together with inverse-square sum divisibility (from the sum-of-squares formula and residue-fiber cancellation), gives \(G_c-G_0\) to order \(3m-v_p(3)\) and the stronger cubic relation \(G_2G_0^2-G_1^3\equiv0\pmod{p^{3m+3}}\). Combining these with the level-independent congruences for the lower-level binomial coefficients modulo \(p^3\), while the factor \(3\) exactly compensates the exceptional \(p=3\) valuation, makes the linear error terms cancel and leaves the desired divisibility.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 C_j(m):=\binom{j p^m}{p^m}\qquad (j=2,3),
\]
and put
\[
 a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^2-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq 3\) and every \(r\geq2\),
\[
 p^{3r+3}\mid a(p^{r-1})-a(p^r).
\]
This is equivalent to the stated congruence.

Throughout the proof set
\[
 w=\begin{cases}1,&p=3,\\0,&p\ne3.\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(w=v_p(3)\), and in particular \(w\leq1\) and \(p^w\mid3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Reduced-residue products
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(m\geq1\), let
\[
 T_m=\{t:0\leq t<p^m,\ p\nmid t\}.
\]
For an integer \(c\), define
\[
 G_m(c)=\prod_{t\in T_m}(t+c p^m).
\]
Notice that
\[
 G_m(0)=\prod_{t\in T_m}t
\]
is not divisible by \(p\).

We shall establish the following two estimates:
\[
 p^{3m-w}\mid G_m(c)-G_m(0)\qquad(c=1,2,\ m\geq1), \tag{1}
\]
and the sharper combined estimate
\[
 p^{3m+3}\mid G_m(2)G_m(0)^2-G_m(1)^3\qquad(m\geq2). \tag{2}
\]
The extra three powers in (2) are the key to the conjecture.

It is convenient to prove these statements in the ring \(\mathbb Z_p\) of \(p\)-adic integers. Every \(t\in T_m\) is a unit there. Write
\[
 x=p^m,
\qquad
 F_m(c)=\prod_{t\in T_m}\left(1+\frac{cx}{t}\right).
\]
Then
\[
 G_m(c)=G_m(0)F_m(c). \tag{3}
\]
Because \(G_m(0)\) is a \(p\)-adic unit, divisibility estimates for the normalized products immediately give the corresponding integer estimates for the \(G_m(c)\).

We will repeatedly use two elementary product facts. If every \(u_t\) is divisible by \(d\), then
\[
 \prod_t(1+u_t)-1-\sum_tu_t
\]
is divisible by \(d^2\), since every omitted term is a product of at least two of the \(u_t\). More generally, suppose \(d\mid u_t,v_t\) and \(d^2\mid u_t-v_t\) for all \(t\). Then
\[
 \prod_t(1+u_t)-\prod_t(1+v_t)-\sum_t(u_t-v_t) \tag{4}
\]
is divisible by \(d^3\). Indeed, expand both products. Their linear terms give the displayed sum. A term of degree at least two in the difference can be written by replacing factors one at a time; it then contains one difference \(u_t-v_t\), divisible by \(d^2\), and at least one further factor divisible by \(d\). Terms of degree at least three are plainly divisible by \(d^3\). This proves (4).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. A reciprocal-square sum
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define in \(\mathbb Z_p\)
\[
 \Sigma_2(m)=\sum_{t\in T_m}\frac1{t^2}.
\]
We claim
\[
 p^{m-w}\mid \Sigma_2(m). \tag{5}
\]

First consider the ordinary integer sum
\[
 S_m=\sum_{t\in T_m}t^2.
\]
Separating from \(0,1,\ldots,p^m-1\) the terms divisible by \(p\), and using
\[
 6\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}j^2=(N-1)N(2N-1),
\]
gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
6S_m
 &=6\sum_{t=0}^{p^m-1}t^2-6p^2\sum_{s=0}^{p^{m-1}-1}s^2\\
 &=p^m\Bigl((p^m-1)(2p^m-1)
 -p(p^{m-1}-1)(2p^{m-1}-1)\Bigr).
\end{aligned} \tag{6}
\]
If \(p\ne3\), then \(p\ge5\), so \(p\) is coprime to \(6\), and (6) yields \(p^m\mid S_m\). If \(p=3\), cancel one factor \(3\) from the factor \(6\) in (6); the remaining factor \(2\) is coprime to \(3\), and one obtains \(3^{m-1}\mid S_m\). Thus in all cases
\[
 p^{m-w}\mid S_m. \tag{7}
\]

Modulo \(p^m\), inversion permutes the reduced residue classes \(T_m\). Therefore
\[
 \sum_{t\in T_m}t^{-2}\equiv\sum_{t\in T_m}t^2=S_m\pmod {p^m}. \tag{8}
\]
Combining (7) and (8) proves (5).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. The ordinary level estimate
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The involution \(t\mapsto x-t\) permutes \(T_m\). Pairing the product defining \(F_m(c)\) with its reindexed copy gives
\[
 F_m(c)^2
 =\prod_{t\in T_m}
 \left(1+\frac{cx}{t}\right)
 \left(1+\frac{cx}{x-t}\right).
\]
Since
\[
 \frac1t+\frac1{x-t}=\frac{x}{t(x-t)},
\]
each paired factor is
\[
 1+\gamma_c(t),
 \qquad
 \gamma_c(t)=(c^2+c)\frac{x^2}{t(x-t)}. \tag{9}
\]
Every \(\gamma_c(t)\) is divisible by \(x^2=p^{2m}\). Hence the terms of degree at least two in \(\prod(1+\gamma_c(t))\) are divisible by \(p^{4m}\).

For the linear sum, use
\[
 \frac1{t(x-t)}
 =-\frac1{t^2}+x\frac1{t^2(x-t)}. \tag{10}
\]
Thus
\[
 \sum_{t\in T_m}\frac1{t(x-t)}
 =-\Sigma_2(m)+xR_m

after defining the integral \(p\)-adic quantity
\[
 R_m=\sum_{t\in T_m}\frac1{t^2(x-t)}.
\]
By (5), the right side of (10), after summation, is divisible by \(p^{m-w}\). Consequently the linear sum of the \(\gamma_c(t)\) is divisible by
\[
 p^{2m}p^{m-w}=p^{3m-w}.
\]
Also \(4m\ge3m-w\) for \(m\ge1\). It follows that
\[
 p^{3m-w}\mid F_m(c)^2-1. \tag{11}
\]
Moreover, directly from the definition, \(F_m(c)\equiv1\pmod p\). Since \(p\ge3\), this implies
\[
 F_m(c)+1\equiv2\not\equiv0\pmod p,
\]
so \(F_m(c)+1\) is a \(p\)-adic unit. Factoring
\[
 F_m(c)^2-1=(F_m(c)-1)(F_m(c)+1)
\]
and cancelling this unit in (11) gives
\[
 p^{3m-w}\mid F_m(c)-1. \tag{12}
\]
Using (3), and then returning from \(\mathbb Z_p\) to integers, proves (1).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The sharper comparison
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(m\ge2\), define
\[
 D_m=\sum_{t\in T_m}\frac1{t^2(x-t)^2}.
\]
We first show
\[
 p\mid D_m. \tag{13}
\]
Modulo \(p\), the summand is a function only of the residue class of \(t\), because \(x=p^m\equiv0\pmod p\), so it becomes
\[
 \frac1{(t(-t))^2}.
\]
Each nonzero residue modulo \(p\) occurs exactly \(p^{m-1}\) times among the elements of \(T_m\). Since \(m\ge2\), this multiplicity is divisible by \(p\). Therefore the whole sum is zero modulo \(p\), proving (13).

Set
\[
 g_t=\gamma_1(t)=2\frac{x^2}{t(x-t)}.
\]
From (9), \(\gamma_2(t)=6x^2/[t(x-t)]=3g_t\). We have
\[
 F_m(2)^2=\prod_{t\in T_m}(1+3g_t), \tag{14}
\]
while
\[
 F_m(1)^6=\left(F_m(1)^2\right)^3
 =\prod_{t\in T_m}(1+g_t)^3. \tag{15}
\]
Apply the product comparison (4), with
\[
 d=x^2,
\quad u_t=3g_t,
\quad v_t=(1+g_t)^3-1.
\]
Both \(u_t\) and \(v_t\) are divisible by \(x^2\), and
\[
 u_t-v_t
 =3g_t-(3g_t+3g_t^2+g_t^3)
 =-3g_t^2-g_t^3, \tag{16}
\]
which is divisible by \(x^4=d^2\). Therefore, by (4), the difference between the products in (14) and (15), minus the sum of (16), is divisible by
\[
 d^3=x^6=p^{6m}. \tag{17}
\]

The sum of the quadratic part in (16) is
\[
 -3\sum_tg_t^2
 =-12x^4\sum_t\frac1{t^2(x-t)^2}
 =-12x^4D_m. \tag{18}
\]
By (13), this is divisible by \(p^{4m+1}\). Every cubic term \(g_t^3\) is divisible by \(x^6=p^{6m}\). For \(m\ge2\),
\[
 6m\ge3m+3,
 \qquad
 4m+1\ge3m+3.
\]
Equations (14)--(18) therefore yield
\[
 p^{3m+3}\mid F_m(2)^2-F_m(1)^6. \tag{19}
\]
Both \(F_m(2)\) and \(F_m(1)\) are congruent to \(1\pmod p\), so
\[
 F_m(2)+F_m(1)^3\equiv2\pmod p
\]
is a unit. Cancelling it from
\[
 F_m(2)^2-F_m(1)^6
 =\bigl(F_m(2)-F_m(1)^3\bigr)
  \bigl(F_m(2)+F_m(1)^3\bigr)
\]
gives
\[
 p^{3m+3}\mid F_m(2)-F_m(1)^3. \tag{20}
\]
Finally, multiplying (20) by \(G_m(0)^3\) and using (3) gives exactly (2):
\[
 G_m(0)^3\bigl(F_m(2)-F_m(1)^3\bigr)
 =G_m(2)G_m(0)^2-G_m(1)^3.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Exact binomial identities between adjacent levels
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next relate the products \(G_m(c)\) to binomial coefficients.

For a positive integer \(L\), let
\[
 Q(L)=\prod_{\substack{1\le k\le L\\p\nmid k}}k.
\]
Separating the multiples of \(p\) from the other factors in \((qp)!\) gives
\[
 (qp)!=p^q q!\,Q(qp). \tag{21}
\]
Also, for \(m\ge1\), splitting the interval \(1,\ldots,a p^m\) into the blocks
\[
 jp^m+1,\ldots,(j+1)p^m\qquad(0\le j<a)
\]
and retaining only terms not divisible by \(p\) gives
\[
 Q(a p^m)=\prod_{j=0}^{a-1}G_m(j). \tag{22}
\]
Indeed, every integer in such a block which is not divisible by \(p\) has a unique form \(t+jp^m\) with \(t\in T_m\).

Let \(n=p^{m-1}\), so \(p^m=np\). Apply (21) to the factorial formula
\[
 \binom{3p^m}{p^m}
 =\frac{(3p^m)!}{(p^m)!(2p^m)!}.
\]
The powers of \(p\) and the smaller factorials cancel, leaving, by (22),
\[
 C_3(m)\,G_m(0)=C_3(m-1)\,G_m(2). \tag{23}
\]
Explicitly, the coprime products in the denominator are
\[
 Q(p^m)=G_m(0),
 \quad
 Q(2p^m)=G_m(0)G_m(1),
\]
and the numerator has
\[
 Q(3p^m)=G_m(0)G_m(1)G_m(2),
\]
which proves (23) after cancellation. In exactly the same way,
\[
 C_2(m)\,G_m(0)=C_2(m-1)\,G_m(1). \tag{24}
\]

Because \(p\nmid G_m(0)\), (1), (23), and (24) imply
\[
 p^{3m}\mid C_3(m)-C_3(m-1), \tag{25}
\]
and
\[
 p^{3m-w}\mid C_2(m)-C_2(m-1). \tag{26}
\]
For (25), when \(p=3\) one needs one additional factor of \(3\). It comes from
\[
 p^w\mid C_3(m-1). \tag{27}
\]
When \(p\ne3\), this is vacuous because \(w=0\). When \(p=3\), it says
\[
 3\mid\binom{3\cdot3^k}{3^k}.
\]
This follows, for example, from the base-\(3\) digit form of Lucas's theorem: the least significant digit of \(3^{k+1}\) and of \(3^k\) is zero, and after dividing both arguments by \(3\) one reduces inductively to \(\binom31=3\equiv0\pmod3\). Multiplying the estimate (1) for \(c=2\) by (27), and then cancelling the \(p\)-unit \(G_m(0)\) in (23), proves (25).

Likewise, Lucas's theorem gives
\[
 C_2(k)=\binom{2p^k}{p^k}\equiv2\pmod p. \tag{28}
\]
Indeed, repeatedly delete the terminal zero base-\(p\) digits and reduce to \(\binom21=2\). Since \(p\ge3\), (28) also shows that every \(C_2(k)\) is a \(p\)-adic unit.

We also need a mixed consequence of the sharp estimate (2). Put
\[
 A=C_3(m),\quad a_0=C_3(m-1),\quad
 B=C_2(m),\quad b_0=C_2(m-1).
\]
Using (23) and (24), we have
\[
 A G_m(0)=a_0G_m(2),
 \qquad
 B G_m(0)=b_0G_m(1).
\]
Multiplying (2) by \(a_0b_0^3\) and substituting these identities gives
\[
 p^{3m+3}\mid G_m(0)^3\bigl(A b_0^3-a_0B^3\bigr).
\]
Since \(G_m(0)\) is prime to \(p\), it may be cancelled, yielding
\[
 p^{3m+3}\mid A b_0^3-a_0B^3. \tag{29}
\]

Finally, telescoping (25) from level \(0\), where \(C_3(0)=3\), gives
\[
 p^3\mid C_3(j)-3 \qquad(j\ge0), \tag{30}
\]
because the step from level \(k-1\) to level \(k\) is divisible by \(p^{3k}\), hence by \(p^3\).

Similarly, multiply (26) by \(3\). Since \(p^w\mid3\), the level-\(k\) difference then becomes divisible by \(p^{3k}\), hence by \(p^3\). Telescoping from \(C_2(0)=2\) gives
\[
 p^3\mid3\bigl(C_2(j)-2\bigr). \tag{31}
\]
This formulation includes the exceptional prime \(3\) without any loss.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Final algebraic assembly
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Fix \(r\ge2\), and abbreviate
\[
 A=C_3(r),\quad a_0=C_3(r-1),
 \qquad
 B=C_2(r),\quad b_0=C_2(r-1).
\]
Set
\[
 \alpha=A-a_0,
 \qquad
 \beta=B-b_0,
 \qquad
 K=3r+3.
\]
The preceding results give:
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
 p\nmid b_0, &\text{by (28)},\\[2mm]
 p^3\mid a_0-3, &\text{by (30)},\\[2mm]
 p^3\mid3(b_0-2), &\text{by (31)},\\[2mm]
 p^{3r}\mid\alpha, &\text{by (25)},\\[2mm]
 p^{3r}\mid3\beta, &\text{by (26) and }p^w\mid3,\\[2mm]
 p^K\mid A b_0^3-a_0B^3, &\text{by (29)}.
\end{array} \tag{32}
\]

From \(p^{3r}\mid3\beta\), one can always remove the possible factor of \(p\) in \(3\), obtaining
\[
 p^{3r-1}\mid\beta. \tag{33}
\]
For \(p\ne3\), in fact \(p^{3r}\mid\beta\); for \(p=3\), (33) follows by cancelling one factor \(3\). Since \(r\ge2\), (32)--(33) imply
\[
 p^K\mid\alpha^2,\qquad
 p^K\mid\beta^2,\qquad
 p^K\mid\beta^3, \tag{34}
\]
because
\[
 6r\ge3r+3,
 \quad
 2(3r-1)\ge3r+3,
 \quad
 3(3r-1)\ge3r+3.
\]

Expand \(B=b_0+\beta\) and \(A=a_0+\alpha\). Modulo \(p^K\), the last line of (32), together with (34), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
0&\equiv A b_0^3-a_0B^3\\
 &=\alpha b_0^3-3a_0b_0^2\beta
   -3a_0b_0\beta^2-a_0\beta^3\\
 &\equiv \alpha b_0^3-3a_0b_0^2\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\nmid b_0\), we may cancel \(b_0^2\), obtaining
\[
 \alpha b_0-3a_0\beta\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{35}
\]

Next,
\[
 3a_0\beta-9\beta=3(a_0-3)\beta.
\]
The factors on the right are divisible respectively by \(p^3\) and, because \(p^{3r}\mid3\beta\), by \(p^{3r}\). Hence their product is divisible by \(p^{3r+3}=p^K\). Adding this to (35) yields
\[
 \alpha b_0-9\beta\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{36}
\]
Multiplying by \(3\),
\[
 3\alpha b_0-27\beta\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{37}
\]

On the other hand,
\[
 3\alpha b_0-6\alpha=\alpha\,3(b_0-2).
\]
Here \(p^{3r}\mid\alpha\) and \(p^3\mid3(b_0-2)\), so
\[
 3\alpha b_0-6\alpha\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{38}
\]
Subtracting (38) from (37) gives
\[
 6\alpha-27\beta\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{39}
\]
Also
\[
 2a_0\alpha-6\alpha=2\alpha(a_0-3)

equiv0\pmod {p^K}, \tag{40}
\]
using \(p^{3r}\mid\alpha\) and \(p^3\mid a_0-3\). Adding (39) and (40), we obtain
\[
 2a_0\alpha-27\beta\equiv0\pmod {p^K},
\]
or equivalently
\[
 27\beta-2a_0\alpha\equiv0\pmod {p^K}. \tag{41}
\]

Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(a_0^2-27b_0)-(A^2-27B)
 &=a_0^2-(a_0+\alpha)^2+27\beta\\
 &=27\beta-2a_0\alpha-\alpha^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The first two terms on the last line are divisible by \(p^K\) by (41), and \(\alpha^2\) is divisible by \(p^K\) by (34). Therefore
\[
 p^{3r+3}\mid
 \bigl(C_3(r-1)^2-27C_2(r-1)\bigr)
 -\bigl(C_3(r)^2-27C_2(r)\bigr).
\]
Since these two expressions are respectively \(a(p^{r-1})\) and \(a(p^r)\), this is precisely
\[
 a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
The proof covers every prime \(p\ge3\), including \(p=3\), and every \(r\ge2\).
